Foundations: Choosing, Powering and Organising Your Space

Before you rent, build or buy anything, you need to know what space your production really needs, what it will cost to run and how much electricity your equipment draws. This module takes you from measuring your current corner to choosing a setup model, sizing your power supply safely and setting the 5S house rules that keep a small workshop working.
From kitchen table to workshop: measuring and choosing a space
Measure a room and calculate its floor area in square metres
Draw a movement (spaghetti) map of how you work today

Most makers start where there is room: a kitchen table, a bedroom corner, a veranda. That works until orders grow. Then you see the limits: materials stored in three places, children walking through wet work, an iron and a sewing machine fighting for the same socket, and hours lost carrying things back and forth. A **workshop** is simply a space arranged around your production, so that work moves smoothly and safely from raw material to finished product.

This course is for any small producer who makes physical goods: bags, furniture, clothing, cosmetics, cleaning products, crafts or packaged food. The examples use different trades, but the methods are the same. Bigger is not automatically better. A well-arranged 20 square metre room often produces more than a cluttered 40 square metre one, because people walk less, search less and wait less.
People building and arranging a structure
Setting up a workshop is a building project: measure and plan first, spend second.
Step 1: measure what you have

Use a tape measure in metres. Measure the length and width of the floor at its widest points, then multiply: **length x width = floor area in square metres (m²)**. Mark on a rough sketch where the door opens, where the windows are, where the sockets and the distribution board (fuse box) are, and where any water point or drain is. These fixed features decide your layout more than any table or shelf, because they are expensive or impossible to move.
Step 2: map how you move today

A **spaghetti diagram** is a sketch of your space with a line drawn every time you walk from one place to another during one batch of work. It is called spaghetti because, in a poorly arranged room, the lines tangle like cooked spaghetti. Count the trips and estimate the distance of each. The long, repeated lines show you exactly what to move closer together. You do not need software: a pencil, paper and a phone timer are enough.
Worked example: measuring a room and finding wasted walking

For example, Chiamaka makes ankara and leather bags in Enugu. She has been offered a back room in her family house and wants to know if it is big enough, and what her current way of working costs her.
She measures the room: 5.0 m long and 4.5 m wide. Area = 5.0 x 4.5 = 22.5 m².
She marks the door on the short wall, one window facing the yard, two double sockets and the fuse box beside the door.

In her current corner, fabric is kept in a wardrobe in another room. During one batch she walks from her cutting table to the wardrobe 12 times, about 8 m there and back each time: 12 x 8 = 96 m per batch.
In the new room she plans a shelf right beside the cutting table, about 1 m away, so each round trip is about 2 m: 12 x 2 = 24 m per batch.
The saving is 96 - 24 = 72 m per batch. She cuts about 5 batches a day, so she saves 72 x 5 = 360 m of walking every day.
The 22.5 m² room is workable, and simply placing fabric storage beside the cutting table removes about 360 m of walking a day. That is time she can spend sewing.

Before you spend, check you are ready. You should be able to answer three questions with numbers: what equipment your process needs, what the space will cost to set up and run each month, and whether your current orders can carry that cost. If you cannot yet answer the third, start with the **minimum setup that lets you produce reliably** and expand one zone at a time as orders grow. Space and machines bought too early tie up money you may need for materials.

A shared workshop sits between the two: lower cost than renting alone, but you must agree schedules and storage.

A **shared workshop or cluster** (several producers in one building, or a cooperative space) splits rent and lets you use equipment you could not afford alone. The cost is coordination: you need written agreements on schedules, storage and who pays for repairs. Whatever model you pick, compare it over a full year, not just the first month, because in many Nigerian towns landlords ask for a year's rent in advance.
Worked example: comparing three options over 12 months
For example, Chiamaka in Enugu compares three options for her bag business. All prices are her own quotes and are approximate.

Home room: one-time setup about 150,000 naira (shelves, a wiring check, a lockable door) and about 15,000 naira a month extra electricity and fuel. Year cost = 150,000 + (15,000 x 12) = 330,000 naira.

Rented shop unit: rent of about 600,000 naira for the year paid upfront, setup about 250,000 naira, running costs about 25,000 naira a month. Year cost = 600,000 + 250,000 + (25,000 x 12) = 1,150,000 naira.
Shared cluster workshop: joining fee and her own shelving about 80,000 naira, then about 30,000 naira a month fee plus 10,000 naira for power. Year cost = 80,000 + (40,000 x 12) = 560,000 naira.
She checks her orders: she sells about 450 bags a month and the extra space is mainly needed for storage and a second machinist.

The home room costs 330,000 naira a year, the shared workshop 560,000 and the shop unit 1,150,000. She chooses the home room now, with a written plan to move to the cluster when she adds a third machine.
Your equipment and power list

List every machine and appliance, and copy its **power rating in watts (W)** from the rating plate or label. Add them up: this is your **total load**. To find the current, divide watts by the supply voltage. Nigerian mains supply is nominally 230 volts, so **current (amps) = watts / 230**. Compare this with the rating of the socket circuit and the cable; an electrician can tell you what your circuits are rated for. Never guess.

Worked example: current and generator size
For example, Chiamaka uses the equipment in the table above and needs a generator for the hours when grid power is off.
Total load = 2,300 W. Current at 230 V = 2,300 / 230 = 10 amps.
She adds a 25% margin, because motors draw extra power for a moment when they start: 2,300 x 1.25 = 2,875 W.
Generators are often rated in kVA. A common working rule is that usable watts are about 0.8 x the kVA figure, so she needs about 2,875 / 0.8 = 3,594 VA, roughly a 3.6 kVA set or larger.
Alternatively, she schedules ironing for times when only one machine is running, which lowers her peak load and lets a smaller set cope.
Her peak load draws about 10 amps. She either buys a generator of at least about 3.6 kVA or plans her loads so the iron and both machines never run together on generator power.
Electrical and generator safety

Give each heavy appliance (iron, heater, kettle, motor) its own socket; do not chain extension boards together. Check plugs and cables before use and remove anything with cracked casing, exposed wires or scorch marks. Ask your electrician to fit a residual current device (RCD) rated at no more than 30 mA, which cuts the power quickly in some types of electric shock, and press its test button regularly. Run generators **outdoors only**, well away from doors and windows, because their exhaust contains carbon monoxide, a gas you cannot see or smell that can kill. Switch off and let the generator cool before refuelling, and store fuel in a proper closed container away from the workshop.
An electric plug
Every machine in your power list needs a safe socket of its own, not a chain of extension boards.

House rules and 5S: organising the space so it stays organised
Explain the five steps of 5S and apply them to a real work area
Run a red-tag sort to clear items that do not belong
Set up labels, shadow boards and fixed homes for tools and materials
Write five non-negotiable workshop rules and teach them on day one

A workshop does not stay organised by accident. Within weeks, offcuts pile up, tools wander and shelves fill with things nobody needs. As the owner, you are now an operations leader: you decide the standards before you are under pressure, and you teach them to everyone who works in the space. The most widely used method for this is **5S**, which came from Japanese manufacturing and is now used in workshops of every size.
The 5S cycle
Sort
Set in order
Shine
Standardise
Sustain
5S is a cycle: after Sustain, you sort again, because clutter always returns.
The five steps
**Sort:** remove everything that is not needed for current work. Broken tools, old samples and materials for products you no longer make go out or into a separate store.
**Set in order:** give every remaining item a fixed home, near where it is used. The things you use most go between waist and shoulder height.
**Shine:** clean the area and the equipment, and use cleaning as an inspection: while wiping a machine you notice the frayed cable or the oil leak.
**Standardise:** write it down and make it visible. Labels on shelves, outlines on tool boards, a photo of how the bench should look at the end of the day.
**Sustain:** keep it going with a short daily routine and a weekly check, led by you until it becomes habit.
Red tags, labels and shadow boards

During Sort, put a red tag (a strip of red tape with the date) on anything you are unsure about and move it to one holding area. If nobody needs it within a month, sell it, give it away or dispose of it safely. For Set in order, a **shadow board** is a board on the wall where each tool hangs over its painted or drawn outline. A missing tool is visible at a glance. Clear plastic boxes with written labels on the front work well for small parts such as zips, screws or bottle caps.
Worked example: what searching costs
For example, Kemi runs a small furniture finishing workshop in Ibadan with two helpers. Tools live wherever they were last used.
For one week she asks each person to note roughly how long they spend looking for tools or materials. They average about 15 minutes a day each.
Three people x 15 minutes = 45 minutes lost every day.
Over 26 working days: 45 x 26 = 1,170 minutes, which is 1,170 / 60 = 19.5 hours a month.
She spends one Saturday morning on 5S: red-tags 23 items, builds a shadow board for hand tools from plywood, and labels every shelf.
She adds a 10 minute end-of-day reset: tools back on the board, floor swept, offcuts in the bin.
Almost 20 hours a month of searching is replaced by 10 minutes a day of reset, and missing tools are now noticed the same day.
A hammer and a wrench
Tools with a fixed, labelled home are found in seconds and missed immediately.
Your non-negotiables
Some rules protect people and property, so they are never optional. Decide them now, write them on one page and put it on the wall. Good non-negotiables are short and checkable. For example:
Making Sustain stick: a weekly 5S score

Sustain is the step most workshops lose. A simple fix is a weekly score. Every Friday, walk the workshop with a helper and give each S a mark from 1 (poor) to 5 (excellent), for a total out of 25. Write the score on a sheet by the door with the date. The number itself matters less than the trend: if it drops two weeks in a row, find out why. Perhaps a new material has no home yet, or the end-of-day reset is being skipped when orders are heavy. Rotate who does the scoring so everyone learns to see the space through the owner's eyes.
Label shelves with what goes there, not just what is there today.
Mark where bins, trolleys and the extinguisher stand with tape on the floor, so an empty spot is obvious.
Keep a photo of the correct layout of each bench pinned at that bench.
Store heavy items low and light, rarely used items high.
The exit route and the fire extinguisher are never blocked, not even for five minutes.
No machine or heat source is left switched on and unattended.
Chemicals stay in their labelled containers, never in drink bottles.
Anyone who spills, breaks or notices a hazard reports it immediately.
The last person out switches off at the main switch and locks up.
Train it on day one

Walk every new worker or apprentice through the space before they start production: where things live, why each zone is placed where it is, and what the non-negotiables are. Then ask them to find five items and put them back. Rules taught on the first day stick far better than rules introduced after the first accident.

Layout, Safety Systems and Capacity

Here you turn your space into a working system. You will draw a zoned floor plan to scale that follows your real production flow, build a simple risk assessment covering fire, electricity, ventilation, chemicals and first aid, and calculate what your workshop can actually produce and what it must produce to pay for itself.
Drawing a zoned floor plan that follows your production flow
Break your process into stages and turn each stage into a zone
Allocate floor area to each zone so the total matches the room
Draw the plan to scale on squared paper
Choose between a straight-line and a U-shaped flow

A good layout is designed around how the product moves, not around where the furniture happens to fit. Write your process as a list of stages, from the moment materials arrive to the moment finished goods leave. Each stage becomes a **zone**. Arrange the zones in the same order, so materials travel in one general direction instead of criss-crossing the room. Criss-crossing wastes time and causes mix-ups, such as a finished item picking up dust or a rejected item being packed by mistake.
Typical workshop zones in order
Receive and store materials
Prepare and cut
Make or assemble
Finish and inspect
Pack and store finished goods
Arrange zones in the order the product moves, so work flows one way through the room.
Rules for placing zones
**Receiving near the door** that materials come in by, so heavy rolls, sacks or drums are not carried through the work area.
**Keep raw materials and finished goods apart.** Use separate shelves on opposite sides of the room if you can.
**Put dusty, hot or smelly work near a window or outside wall,** with an extractor fan blowing out, and away from finishing and packing.
**Place machines near sockets** so no cable crosses a walkway.
**Keep one clear walkway** from every work position to the exit, and never store anything in it.
**Give waste a home** in each zone: an offcut bin at cutting, a rag bin at finishing.
Straight line or U-shape?

In a **straight-line flow**, materials enter at one end of the room and leave at the other. It suits long, narrow rooms and rooms with two doors. In a **U-shaped flow**, work goes down one side, across the end and back up the other side, so it finishes near where it started. This suits rooms with one door, because receiving and dispatch are both near the entrance, and it lets one person easily help at two neighbouring stations.
Worked example: zoning a 24 m² bag workshop
For example, Hauwa in Kano is moving her bag making into a room 6 m long and 4 m wide with one door. Her process: receive fabric and leather, cut, sew on two machines, finish and check, pack.
Room area = 6 x 4 = 24 m². She chooses a U-shape because there is only one door.
She allocates space, including standing room: receiving and raw store 3.5 m², cutting 5 m², sewing (two machines) 6 m², finishing and inspection 3 m², packing and finished store 3 m², walkway 3.5 m².
She checks the total: 3.5 + 5 + 6 + 3 + 3 + 3.5 = 24 m², which matches the room.
She puts the sewing machines along the wall with the two double sockets, and the cutting table under the window for good light.
On squared paper she uses a scale of 1 square (1 cm) = 50 cm, so the room is drawn 12 squares long and 8 squares wide.
Every square metre has a job, the zones follow the product, and her plan fits on one sheet she can show a carpenter, an electrician or a buyer.

Sizing each workstation

A zone needs more floor than the furniture in it. Measure each table, machine and shelf, then add room for the person to stand, move and handle materials. A cutting table that you work around on two sides needs space on both of those sides; a sewing machine needs room for the chair to push back and for bundles of cut pieces beside it; a shelf needs space in front to open boxes and lift safely. Work at the height of the task: a table that is too low for cutting causes back pain across a long day, and raising it on blocks is cheap.
**Common mistake:** storing finished goods in the walkway "just for today". It becomes permanent and blocks the exit.
**Common mistake:** placing the dustiest or smelliest task furthest from the window because that is where there was space.
**Common mistake:** no space for work waiting between stages, so piles end up on the floor.
**Common mistake:** a door that swings into a workstation. Mark door arcs on the plan.

Before paying a carpenter, mark the zones on the real floor with masking tape or chalk and run one batch of work through it. You will find problems in an hour that a drawing hides, such as a door that hits the cutting table or a shelf you cannot reach.

Risk assessment: fire, electricity, ventilation, chemicals and first aid
Identify hazards in your workshop and score their risk
Choose controls using the hierarchy of control
Apply recognised precautions for fire, electricity, ventilation and chemical storage
Set up a first aid kit, a daily check and an incident log

A **hazard** is anything that could cause injury or illness: a sharp blade, a flammable liquid, a trailing cable. **Risk** is how likely it is that someone is harmed, and how badly. A risk assessment has three steps, as the UK Health and Safety Executive (HSE) sets out in its simple guidance for small businesses: identify the hazards, judge the risk, then remove the hazard or control it. You do not need a consultant for a small workshop, but you do need to write it down and review it when anything changes.
Scoring and prioritising

A simple method is to score **likelihood** from 1 (unlikely) to 3 (likely) and **severity** from 1 (minor injury) to 3 (serious injury or death). Multiply them. A score of 6 or 9 needs action now; 3 or 4 needs action soon; 1 or 2 is watched. This scoring is a tool for setting priorities, not an exact measurement.
Worked example: a furniture finishing workshop
For example, Kemi in Ibadan sands, stains and lacquers furniture with two helpers. She walks the workshop with a notebook and lists hazards.
Lacquer thinner stored beside a hot plate used for glue: likelihood 3 x severity 3 = 9.
Fine dust from sanding with the window closed: 3 x 2 = 6.
Extension cable running across the walkway to the sander: 2 x 2 = 4.
Chisels left loose on the bench: 2 x 2 = 4.

She acts on the highest first: the thinner moves to a closed metal cabinet on the far side of the room, the hot plate is replaced with a glue method that needs no flame, sanding moves next to the open window with an extractor fan blowing out and dust masks are provided, the sander gets a socket on its own wall, and chisels get a rack.
Her two highest risks are removed or reduced the same week, and she reviews the list whenever she adds a new process or machine.
Hierarchy of control
Eliminate the hazard
Substitute something safer
Engineering controls
Rules and training
Protective equipment
Work from the top: removing a hazard beats managing it, and protective equipment is the last line of defence.
Fire

Fire needs three things: **heat** (a spark, flame or hot surface), **fuel** (anything that burns) and **oxygen**. Remove any one and there is no fire. In workshops, fuel is often less obvious than a can of petrol: packaging, rags, sawdust, offcuts, oils and fine dust from wood, flour or sugar all burn. Keep flammable liquids in small, closed, labelled containers away from any heat source, empty waste bins daily, and keep the exit clear. Keep a suitable extinguisher near the exit, not deep in the room, and learn its type: carbon dioxide (CO2) or dry powder extinguishers can be used on electrical fires; **never use water on an electrical fire or on burning oil**. A fire blanket smothers a small pan or oil fire. Have it serviced as the supplier advises, and post the emergency number (112 in Nigeria) by the door.
Ventilation and chemicals

Fumes from solvents, glues, dyes, bleach and caustic products, and fine dust from sanding or powders, harm the lungs and can make you dizzy. Work with these near an open window with a fan blowing **out**, and put extraction as close to the source as you can. For chemical storage: keep every chemical in its original labelled container, never in a food or drink container; store them low, on a tray that will catch a leak, away from heat and sunlight; keep acids, bleach and other oxidisers apart from each other, because some mixtures release dangerous gases; and keep the supplier's safety data sheet (SDS) on file. Lock chemicals away from children.
First aid kit and first aider

Name one person to take charge of first aid and keep a stocked kit where everyone can reach it. The HSE's suggested minimum kit for low-risk work is: a first aid guidance leaflet, individually wrapped sterile plasters of assorted sizes, sterile eye pads, triangular bandages, safety pins, large and medium sterile unmedicated wound dressings and disposable gloves. Add clean water for rinsing eyes and skin if you use chemicals. A first aid kit is not a medicine cabinet: for anything beyond minor cuts, get the person to a clinic or hospital.
A red fire extinguisher
Keep the extinguisher by the exit so you move towards safety when you reach for it.

Calculate the break-even volume the workshop must produce

Every workshop has a ceiling: the most it can produce with its current space, machines and people. Knowing that number lets you accept orders with confidence, plan expansion before you are turning buyers away, and see whether the space is paying for itself. Two ideas do most of the work: the **bottleneck** and the **break-even volume**.
Finding the bottleneck

Time each stage for one unit with a phone stopwatch, over several units, and take a typical figure. If a stage has more than one worker or machine doing the same job in parallel, divide its time by that number. The stage with the **longest effective time** is the bottleneck. The whole workshop can only go as fast as that stage. Speeding up any other stage just creates a pile of work waiting in front of the bottleneck.
Effective minutes per bag at each stage
Cut: 8 minutes
Sew: 15 minutes (bottleneck)
Finish: 6 minutes
Pack: 4 minutes
Sewing takes longest per bag even with two machines, so it sets the pace for the whole workshop.
Worked example: daily and monthly capacity
For example, Hauwa's bag workshop in Kano. Cutting takes 8 minutes a bag, sewing 30 minutes a bag on each of two machines, finishing 6 minutes and packing 4 minutes.
Effective sewing time = 30 / 2 machines = 15 minutes a bag. This is the longest stage, so sewing is the bottleneck.
The working day is 8 hours with 1 hour of breaks: 7 x 60 = 420 minutes.
Machines are not productive every minute (changing thread, small repairs, power cuts), so she plans at 80%: 420 x 0.8 = 336 productive minutes.
Daily capacity = 336 / 15 = 22.4, so 22 bags a day.
With 24 working days a month: 22 x 24 = 528 bags a month.
She currently sells about 450 bags a month: 450 / 528 = about 85% of capacity.
Her ceiling is about 528 bags a month and she is already using about 85% of it. Any large new order needs more sewing capacity, not more cutting.
One-time costs and running costs

**One-time (setup) costs** are spent once: machines, shelving, wiring work, safety equipment, the first stock of materials. **Running (fixed monthly) costs** come every month whether you produce or not: rent, wages for regular staff, power and fuel, water, cleaning, maintenance. **Variable costs** rise with each unit: materials and packaging. Keep these three separate, or you will mistake a big setup month for a loss-making business.
Worked example: break-even volume
For example, Hauwa lists her monthly running costs and her figures per bag. All amounts are approximate.
Running costs a month: rent 50,000 + power and fuel 60,000 + water and cleaning 8,000 + two machinists' wages 150,000 + maintenance 12,000 = 280,000 naira.
Each bag sells for 6,500 naira. Materials cost 3,200 and packaging 300, so each bag contributes 6,500 - 3,200 - 300 = 3,000 naira towards running costs.
Break-even volume = 280,000 / 3,000 = 93.3, so she must sell 94 bags a month just to cover the workshop.
At 450 bags a month her contribution is 450 x 3,000 = 1,350,000 naira, leaving 1,350,000 - 280,000 = 1,070,000 naira before her own pay, tax and savings.
The workshop needs 94 bags a month to pay for itself, well below her 450 sales. The space is supporting growth, not draining it.
Raising capacity before you spend

Because the bottleneck sets the pace, an hour lost there is an hour lost for the whole workshop, while an hour saved anywhere else changes nothing. Before buying a new machine, try the free improvements, and re-time the bottleneck after each change to see what really worked.
**Keep the bottleneck running:** stagger breaks so a machine at the bottleneck is never idle at lunchtime.
**Feed it ready work:** prepare kits (cut pieces, thread, zips, labels) in advance so the machinist never stops to look for parts.
**Move tasks away from it:** if sewers also attach labels, give that job to the person at a quicker stage.
**Protect it from power cuts:** put the bottleneck machines first on your generator or inverter plan.
**Keep a buffer:** a planned workshop running near 100% of capacity has no room for breakdowns, rush orders or a sick worker, so plan to keep some spare.
Track it for three months

Plans are estimates. Record actual output, actual running costs and actual sales each month for at least three months. If output stays well below capacity, find out why (stock-outs, power cuts, absent staff) before you spend on more space or machines.

Growth, People and Your Expansion Plan

An organised, safe workshop opens doors to bigger buyers and partners, but only if you commit to what your space can really deliver. This module shows you how to judge a large order against capacity, share equipment and capacity with partners, train and organise the people who work with you, and write a 90-day expansion plan with honest cost and payback figures.
Buyer visits, big orders and sharing capacity with partners
Prepare your workshop for a buyer or partner visit
Check whether a large order fits your spare capacity and cash
Compare options when an order is bigger than your capacity
Set out the terms of an equipment or capacity sharing agreement

Wholesale buyers, distributors and institutional customers often want to see where their order will be made, in person or by video. They are asking one question: can this producer deliver the quantity and quality she promises, on time? A clean, zoned, safe workshop answers much of that before you say a word. Your job is to make sure the answer is true, by never promising more than your workshop can produce.
Preparing for a visit
Run a full 5S reset the day before: walkways clear, labels visible, waste out.
Have your floor plan, equipment list and monthly capacity figure on one printed page.
Show the flow: walk the visitor from receiving to packing in order.
Point out safety basics: the extinguisher by the exit, the first aid kit, chemical storage, the daily checklist.
Have three finished samples and your quality checklist ready to show how you inspect.
For remote buyers, record a short walkthrough on your phone in good daylight, following the same route.
Two people shaking hands over a deal
A deal only builds trust if your workshop can actually deliver the quantity you agree.
Does the order fit?

Check three things: **capacity** (spare units per day after your regular orders, multiplied by the working days until delivery), **cash** (materials must usually be bought before the buyer pays), and **quality** (can you keep your standard at the higher speed). If any one fails, do not simply say yes and hope.
Worked example: a 400-bag order in three weeks
For example, a hotel group asks Hauwa for 400 branded bags in 3 weeks (18 working days) at 6,000 naira each. Her workshop makes 22 bags a day, and regular customers already take about 15 a day.
Spare capacity = 22 - 15 = 7 bags a day. Over 18 days: 7 x 18 = 126 bags.
Shortfall = 400 - 126 = 274 bags. She cannot meet the date with the current setup.
Cash: materials and packaging are about 3,500 naira a bag, so 400 x 3,500 = 1,400,000 naira is needed upfront. Order value is 400 x 6,000 = 2,400,000 naira; a 50% deposit would be 1,200,000 naira.
Option A: offer 126 bags by the date and the rest in a second delivery.

Option B: add a third sewing machine. Sewing becomes 30 / 3 = 10 minutes a bag, capacity becomes 336 / 10 = 33 bags a day, spare becomes 33 - 15 = 18 a day, and 400 / 18 = 22.2, so the order takes 23 working days, about 4 weeks.
Option C: subcontract part of the sewing to a trusted producer under a written agreement, with her own final inspection.
She proposes delivery in 4 weeks with a 50% deposit, using a third machine, and puts the terms in writing. Saying no to the impossible date protects the relationship far more than missing it.
Before you accept a big order
Spare capacity covers it
Cash for materials is secured
Quality can be kept
Delivery date is realistic
Terms are in writing
If any box stays unticked, negotiate the date, quantity or deposit before you say yes.
Sharing equipment and capacity
Keeping quality at volume

Big orders fail on quality as often as on time. Before production starts, make a sample and have the buyer approve it in writing; keep the approved sample in the workshop as the standard everyone compares against. Write a short inspection plan, for example checking every bag at finishing for stitching, handles and lining, and opening a set number of packed cartons before dispatch. If you subcontract, the same sample and checklist apply, and you inspect the partner's work yourself before it is mixed with yours.

Put these terms in the written order: product specification and approved sample, quantity, unit price, delivery dates, deposit and balance, how goods will be inspected on delivery, and what happens to rejected items.
Keep every message and document about the order in one folder.

Partnerships with other producers can give you capacity without buying it. Two makers can share an expensive machine, a cluster can run a shared finishing or packing area, or a partner can sew overflow work for you. These arrangements fail when terms are vague. Write a short agreement covering: who owns the equipment; the booking schedule; who pays for power, consumables and repairs; how damage is handled; quality standards and who inspects; how payment is calculated; and how either side can end the arrangement with notice. Both sign and keep a copy.
Protect your cash on large orders

Agree payment terms in writing before you buy materials: a deposit, the balance due on delivery, and what happens if the buyer changes the design or cancels. Confirm any transfer in your own banking app, not from a screenshot or a text alert, before you release goods.
A tidy, safe, zoned workshop helps win buyers, but only honest capacity keeps them.
Spare capacity = daily capacity minus regular orders, multiplied by working days to delivery.

Staffing the workshop: roles, induction, skills matrix and maintenance
Write clear roles and zone responsibilities for each person
Run a structured induction and train tasks in four steps
Build a skills matrix and use it to plan cross-training
Assign routine maintenance so machines do not fail at the worst time

As people join, your space rules become people rules. In a small shared room, confusion about who does what quickly turns into tension, poor quality and accidents. Every person should know four things: their zone and main tasks, the safety standards for those tasks, how shared tools and machines are booked and returned, and who to tell immediately about a problem or hazard.
Induction: the first day
Induction for a new worker
Welcome and house rules
Walk the full flow
Safety and emergency points
Supervised first task
Sign off and review
A planned first day teaches the whole system, not just one isolated task.

Walk the new person through the whole flow, from receiving to packing, so they understand where their work comes from and where it goes. People who see the whole process make better quality decisions than people who only know their own station. Show the exit, the extinguisher, the first aid kit, the main switch and the chemical store, and explain the non-negotiable rules. Treat workers and apprentices fairly: agree pay, hours and duties clearly at the start, preferably in writing.
Training a task in four steps
**Tell:** explain the task, the quality standard and the safety points.
**Show:** do the task slowly while they watch, explaining each key point.
**Do together:** they do it while you watch and correct straight away.
**Check and sign off:** they do it alone to standard, more than once, and you record that they are trained.
The skills matrix

A **skills matrix** is a grid with people down the side and tasks across the top. In each box you mark the level: 0 = not trained, 1 = learning, 2 = can do alone, 3 = can train others. It shows at a glance who can cover for whom, and which tasks depend on a single person. That single person is a risk: if she is sick or leaves, production stops.
Person
Cutting
Sewing
Finishing and QC
Packing
Machine care
Hauwa (owner)
Machinist 1

Apprentice
Worked example: closing the gaps
For example, Hauwa reads the skills matrix above for her bag workshop in Kano.
Only Hauwa is at level 2 or above in cutting and in finishing and quality control. If she travels to buy materials, both stages stop.
She plans to train Machinist 1 in cutting during the slow first week of each month, using the four steps, aiming for level 2 in about 8 weeks.
She trains the apprentice in finishing checks using her written quality checklist.

Machine care: she sets a routine. Each machinist cleans lint and oils her own machine as the manufacturer's manual says at the end of each week, and Machinist 1 checks belts, plugs and cables monthly and records it.
Within two months, two people can cut and two can inspect, and every machine has a named person responsible for its routine care.
Roles and zone owners

Give each zone a named owner. The owner does not do all the work there, but she checks each day that the zone is stocked, clean and safe, and she reports anything that is running low or broken. Write each person's main tasks on one card: the zone she owns, the tasks she does, the safety rules for those tasks, and who she reports to. In a small workshop, the owner of the business often holds several roles; writing them down shows which ones to hand over first as the team grows.
A short daily start

A five-minute standing meeting at the start of each day keeps everyone aligned: today's orders and targets, any machine or material problems, any safety point from yesterday's incident log, and who is covering for anyone absent. Look after basic welfare too: clean drinking water, access to a toilet and handwashing, a place to rest and eat away from chemicals and dust, reasonable working hours and breaks, and enough light and ventilation to work without strain. People who are looked after do safer and better work.

Protective equipment is part of training, not a box of items on a shelf. Show each person which equipment her tasks need, such as gloves, goggles, a dust mask or closed shoes, how to check it for damage, and where to get a replacement. Provide it free, replace it when worn, and lead by example: if the owner skips goggles, everyone will.
Settle shared-space disputes quickly

When two people need the same machine at the same time, or disagree about how an area is kept, make a clear decision and write it into the rules, such as a booking sheet for the shared machine. In a small room, unresolved friction grows fast.

Your workshop portfolio and 90-day expansion plan
Assemble a workshop portfolio that proves operational capability
Choose the expansion that removes your current bottleneck
Calculate the cost, capacity gain and payback period of an expansion
Write a 90-day plan with milestones and training needs

A product portfolio shows what you make. A **workshop portfolio** shows that you can make it reliably, safely and at volume. It speaks to wholesale buyers checking reliability, lenders and grant reviewers checking that money will be used well, and partners deciding whether to share equipment or orders with you.
What goes in the portfolio
Your scaled floor plan with zones and flow arrows, plus clear photos of each zone.
Your equipment list with power ratings and your power plan.
Your capacity figure per day and per month, and how you calculated it.
Your risk assessment summary, non-negotiable rules and daily checklist.
Your skills matrix and induction plan.
One or two improvement stories: a bottleneck you removed or a hazard you fixed, with before and after figures.

Keep the portfolio short and current: a few printed pages in a folder for visitors, and the same pages as photos or a PDF you can send on WhatsApp or email. Date every page and update the capacity figure and photos whenever the layout changes, because an out-of-date plan raises doubts instead of trust.
A person beside a rising growth chart
Expansion should raise your real capacity at the bottleneck, and pay back in a period you can survive.
Choosing what to expand

Expand at the **bottleneck**. A bigger cutting table does nothing if sewing sets the pace. Options include another machine or workstation at the bottleneck, a second shift, a larger space, or partnering for overflow. For each, estimate three numbers: the **one-time cost**, the **extra monthly running cost**, and the **extra contribution** from the additional units you can realistically sell, not just produce. Then calculate the **payback period: one-time cost / extra monthly profit**.
Worked example: is a third machine worth it?
For example, Hauwa considers a third sewing machine for her Kano bag workshop. Prices are approximate quotes.
One-time cost: machine, table and an extra socket fitted by an electrician, about 500,000 naira in total.
Capacity rises from 22 to 33 bags a day: from 22 x 24 = 528 to 33 x 24 = 792 bags a month.
She does not assume she will sell all 792. From her buyer conversations she expects about 60 extra bags a month at first.
Extra contribution: 60 x 3,000 = 180,000 naira a month. Extra running costs: a third machinist at 75,000 plus about 10,000 power = 85,000 naira.
Extra monthly profit = 180,000 - 85,000 = 95,000 naira. Payback = 500,000 / 95,000 = about 5.3 months.
She checks the floor plan: the third machine fits in the sewing zone if the finished goods shelf moves 1 m along the wall.

The machine pays for itself in about five to six months on cautious sales, and it also lets her accept larger orders like the hotel group's. She plans to buy it in month two, once the deposit from that order arrives.
A 90-day expansion plan
Days 1-30: confirm demand, quotes
Days 31-60: buy, install, wire
Days 61-75: hire and train
Days 76-90: run, measure, review
Confirm demand before buying, and leave time to train people before you rely on the new capacity.
Writing the 90-day plan
Funding the expansion

Match the money to the payback. Use savings, retained profit, buyer deposits or supplier credit first where you can, because they carry no interest. If you borrow, check that the monthly repayment is comfortably below the extra monthly profit you expect, even in a weak month, and read every charge before you sign. Never borrow against a full-capacity forecast.
Test the plan against a bad case

Run the payback again with weaker sales. In Hauwa's example, if she sells only 30 extra bags a month, extra contribution is 30 x 3,000 = 90,000 naira against 85,000 naira of extra running costs, leaving just 5,000 naira a month. Payback becomes 500,000 / 5,000 = 100 months. That is why she waits for confirmed orders and a deposit before buying, and why the plan has a review point at day 90.
**Risk:** demand lower than expected. **Response:** buy only after confirmed orders or deposits.
**Risk:** delivery or installation delays. **Response:** get a written delivery date and keep the old setup running.
**Risk:** training takes longer. **Response:** start cross-training before the machine arrives.

For each phase, write the actions, the person responsible, the cost and the evidence that it is done. Include safety: any new machine needs a safe socket, a place in the floor plan that keeps the walkway clear, an update to the risk assessment and training before use. End with the measures you will review at day 90: actual output per day, actual sales, running costs and any incidents.
Be honest about uncertainty

Mark every figure that is an estimate. A plan that says "about 60 extra bags a month, based on three buyer conversations" is more credible to a lender or partner than one that promises the full capacity will sell.
A workshop portfolio proves capability: plan, photos, capacity, safety and people.
Expand at the bottleneck, or the extra spending will not raise output.
Payback = one-time cost / extra monthly profit, using sales you can realistically make.
A 90-day plan needs actions, owners, costs, safety updates, training time and review measures.

Why this matters
Plan the space before you spend
A workshop is space arranged around production
Bigger is not automatically better
Know your costs and your power needs
A workshop is simply a space arranged around your production, so work moves smoothly and safely from raw material to finished product.
Bigger is not automatically better. A well-arranged 20 square metre room often produces more than a cluttered 40 square metre one, because people walk less and search less.
So before you rent or buy anything, measure, count your costs and plan your power.
Step by step
Measure and map before you choose
Judge every room against your written must-solve list.
Measure length and width; area = length x width
Mark doors, windows, sockets, fuse box, drains
Draw a spaghetti diagram of one batch
Check wiring, air, water, access, security, escape
Write the 3 to 5 problems the space must solve
Step one. Measure in metres, and multiply length by width for the floor area.
Step two. Sketch the room and mark the fixed features. They decide your layout, because they are expensive to move.
Step three. Draw a line every time you walk somewhere during one batch. In a poor layout the lines tangle like spaghetti.
For example, Chiamaka in Enugu put a fabric shelf beside her cutting table and saved about 360 metres of walking a day.
Step four. Check any new site. If sockets are scorched or warm, get a qualified electrician to inspect before you sign.
Step five. Write the problems the workshop must fix. A cheap room that fails two of your must-haves is not cheap.
Worked example
Compare the full year, not one month
For example, Chiamaka in Enugu compares three options for her bag business.
Home room, 12 months
Shared cluster, 12 months
Rented shop unit, 12 months
Naira prices are approximate.
Landlords often ask for a year's rent in advance, so compare options over 12 months: one-time costs plus 12 months of running costs.
A room at home costs Chiamaka about 330,000 naira for the year. It is cheap, but family life and work get in each other's way.
A shared cluster workshop costs about 560,000 naira. It splits rent, but needs written agreements on schedules and storage.
A rented shop unit costs about 1,150,000 naira, with the rent paid upfront.
She chooses the home room now, with a written plan to move to the cluster when she adds a third machine.
Your power plan
Work out what your equipment draws
Never guess. Check your circuits with an electrician.
List every machine and its watts from the label
Add them up: this is your total load
Current in amps = watts / 230
Add a 25% margin for motors starting
Generator VA = watts / 0.8
Copy the watts from each machine's label and add them up. Chiamaka's machines, iron, bulbs, fans and charger come to 2,300 watts.
Mains supply is nominally 230 volts, so divide watts by 230 to get amps. That is 10 amps.
Motors draw extra power when they start, so add 25 percent. That gives 2,875 watts.
Usable watts are about 0.8 times a generator's kVA, so she needs roughly a 3.6 kVA set. Or she plans work so the iron and both machines never run together.
Safety first
Heavy appliances get their own socket. Never chain extension boards. Remove cracked or scorched cables.
Ask your electrician for an RCD of no more than 30 mA, and press its test button regularly.
Exhaust has carbon monoxide, which can kill. Cool it before refuelling; store fuel in a closed container.
Give each heavy appliance its own socket, never chain extension boards, and remove any cable with exposed wires or scorch marks.
Ask your electrician to fit a residual current device, an RCD, rated at no more than 30 milliamps. Press its test button regularly.
Run generators outdoors only. The exhaust contains carbon monoxide, a gas you cannot see or smell that can kill. Let it cool before refuelling.
Keep it organised
Sort: remove what is not needed
Set in order: a fixed home for everything
Shine: clean, and inspect while you clean
Standardise: labels, outlines, photos
Sustain: a daily reset and a weekly score
A workshop does not stay organised by accident. Use 5S. Sort: red-tag anything unsure, and if nobody needs it within a month, it goes.
Set in order: a fixed home for everything, near where it is used. A shadow board shows a missing tool at a glance.
Shine: while you wipe a machine, you notice the frayed cable.
Standardise: label shelves and pin a photo of how each bench should look.
Sustain. For example, Kemi in Ibadan replaced about 19.5 hours a month of searching for tools with a 10 minute end-of-day reset.
Non-negotiables
Rules that are never optional
Exit route and extinguisher never blocked
No machine or heat left on and unattended
Chemicals only in labelled containers
Report spills and hazards immediately
Last person out switches off and locks up
Some rules protect people and property, so they are never optional. Write them on one page and put it on the wall.
Keep the exit clear. Never leave heat unattended. Keep chemicals labelled, never in drink bottles. Report hazards at once. Switch off and lock up.
Teach these on day one, before the first accident.
Key points
Remember
Measure, map and list must-solves first
Compare setup options over 12 months
Watts / 230 = amps; add a margin for motors
Generators run outdoors only
5S is a cycle; rules go on the wall
To remember. Measure and map first. Compare options over a full year. Work out your amps and add a margin. Keep generators outdoors.
And keep 5S going, with your rules on the wall.

Module 2 video
Layout, safety and how much your workshop can make
Layout, safety, and how much your workshop can make.
This is the video for module two of Factory and Workshop Setup.
Why this matters
Turn your space into a working system
Zones that follow your product
A written risk assessment
Know your ceiling and your floor
In this module your space becomes a working system. First, a floor plan designed around how the product moves, not where the furniture fits.
Second, a simple written risk assessment for fire, electricity, fumes, chemicals and first aid.
Third, two numbers: the most your workshop can make, and the least it must sell to pay for itself.
Zoning
Zones in the order the product moves
Receive and store materials, near the door
Write your process as stages. Each stage becomes a zone, placed in order, so work flows one way instead of criss-crossing.
Receiving goes near the door, so heavy sacks are not carried through the work.
Put dusty, hot or smelly work near a window with a fan blowing out. Place machines near sockets so no cable crosses a walkway.
Keep raw materials and finished goods apart, and keep one clear walkway to the exit.
A common mistake is storing finished goods in the walkway just for today. It becomes permanent and blocks the exit.
Two shapes
Straight line
In at one end, out at the other
Suits long, narrow rooms
Good with two doors
U-shape
Finishes near where it started
Suits rooms with one door
One person can help two stations
In a straight-line flow, materials enter at one end and leave at the other. It suits long rooms with two doors.
In a U-shape, work goes down one side and back up the other. For example, Hauwa in Kano has a 24 square metre room with one door, so she chose a U-shape.
Draw your plan to scale, then mark the zones on the real floor with tape and run one batch before you pay a carpenter.
Risk assessment
Find hazards, score them, act
Remove a hazard first. Protective equipment is the last line.
Walk the workshop and list the hazards
Score likelihood 1 to 3, severity 1 to 3
Multiply: 6 or 9 means act now
Control the highest score first
Review when anything changes
A hazard is anything that could cause harm. Risk is how likely harm is, and how bad. Walk your workshop with a notebook.
Score likelihood and severity from 1 to 3 and multiply. A score of 6 or 9 needs action now. 3 or 4 needs action soon.
For example, Kemi in Ibadan found lacquer thinner beside a hot plate. That scored 9. She moved the thinner to a closed metal cabinet and replaced the hot plate with a glue method that needs no flame.
Work from the top of the hierarchy of control. Eliminate, then substitute, then engineer, then rules and training. Protective equipment comes last.
Safety systems
Fire, fumes and first aid
Never use water on electrical or oil fires. Extinguisher by the exit. Post 112 by the door.
Fan blowing out. Original labelled containers, stored low. Keep bleach and acids apart.
A named first aider and a stocked kit. Anything beyond minor cuts goes to a clinic.
Fire needs heat, fuel and oxygen. Rags, sawdust and packaging are fuel. Keep flammables away from heat, and keep the extinguisher near the exit.
Never use water on an electrical fire or burning oil. The emergency number in Nigeria is 112.
Work with fumes and dust near an open window with a fan blowing out. Keep every chemical in its labelled original container, never a drink bottle, and keep acids and bleach apart.
Name one person in charge of first aid and keep a stocked kit where everyone can reach it. Write every incident or near miss in a log.
Your ceiling
Find the bottleneck and your capacity
The whole workshop can only go as fast as its bottleneck.
Time each stage for one unit
Divide by parallel machines or workers
Longest time is the bottleneck
Plan on 80% of working minutes
Time each stage with a phone stopwatch. If two machines do the same job, divide by two. Hauwa sews a bag in 30 minutes on each of two machines, so 15 minutes a bag.
Sewing is her longest stage, so it is the bottleneck.
Her day has 420 working minutes. Machines are not productive every minute, so she plans at 80 percent: 336 minutes. That gives 22 bags a day, or 528 bags a month.
Speeding up cutting changes nothing. She needs more sewing time.
Your floor
Hauwa's monthly running costs
For example, Hauwa in Kano lists her running costs. Each bag sells for 6,500 naira.
Rent
Power and fuel
Water and cleaning
Two machinists' wages
Maintenance
Naira prices are approximate.
Running costs come every month, whether you produce or not. Keep them separate from one-time setup costs.
Hauwa pays rent, power and fuel, water and cleaning, two machinists and maintenance.

That is about 280,000 naira a month. Each bag leaves 3,000 naira after materials and packaging. 280,000 divided by 3,000 means she must sell 94 bags a month just to cover the workshop. She sells about 450, so the space is paying for itself.
Key points
Remember
Zones follow the product, one way through
Score hazards and fix the highest first
No water on electrical or oil fires
The bottleneck sets your capacity
Break-even = running costs / contribution

To remember. Zones follow the product. Score hazards and fix the worst first. No water on electrical or oil fires. The bottleneck sets your capacity. And divide running costs by what each unit contributes to find your break-even.

Big orders, your team and a 90-day expansion plan
Big orders, your team, and a 90-day expansion plan.
This is the video for module three of Factory and Workshop Setup.
Why this matters
Grow without breaking promises
Judge a big order against capacity
Train people so work never depends on one
Expand at the bottleneck, with honest payback
A tidy, safe workshop helps you win bigger buyers. But only honest capacity keeps them. Never promise more than your workshop can produce.
As people join, your space rules become people rules.
And when you grow, you spend where it raises output, with figures you can defend.
Hauwa's 400-bag order in 18 days
Saying no to an impossible date beats missing it.
Spare capacity: 22 - 15 = 7 bags a day
Over 18 days: 7 x 18 = 126 bags
Shortfall: 400 - 126 = 274 bags
Offer options: split, add a machine, or partner
For example, a hotel group asks Hauwa for 400 bags in 18 working days. She makes 22 bags a day, and regular customers take 15. So she has 7 spare a day.
Over 18 days, that is 126 bags.
She is short by 274 bags. She cannot meet the date as she is.
So she offers options: deliver 126 now and the rest later, add a third machine and deliver in about 4 weeks, or subcontract to a trusted producer under a written agreement.
She proposes 4 weeks with a 50 percent deposit, in writing.
Before you say yes
Check all five before you say yes. Materials are bought before the buyer pays, so agree a deposit in writing.
Get the sample approved in writing and keep it as the standard. Confirm any transfer in your own banking app, not from a screenshot or text alert, before you release goods.
Training people
Teach any task in four steps
On day one, walk the whole flow and show every safety point.
Tell: the task, the standard, the safety points
Show: do it slowly while they watch
Do together: they do it, you correct
Check and sign off: alone, to standard

On the first day, walk a new person through the whole flow. Show the exit, extinguisher, first aid kit, main switch and chemical store. Then train each task in four steps. Tell: explain the standard and the safety points.
Show: do it slowly while they watch.
Do together: they do it while you watch and correct straight away.
Check and sign off: they do it alone, to standard, more than once, and you record it.
Organising people
Three tools for a small team
People down the side, tasks across the top, scored 0 to 3. Find tasks only one person can do.
Each zone has a named owner who checks daily that it is stocked, clean and safe.
Every machine has a named person for routine care, following the manual.

A skills matrix scores each person on each task, from 0, not trained, to 3, can train others. Hauwa saw that only she could cut and inspect. If she travels, both stages stop. So she is cross-training a machinist and the apprentice.
Give each zone a named owner, who reports anything running low or broken.
And give every machine a named person for its routine care. Provide protective equipment free, and wear it yourself. If the owner skips goggles, everyone will.
Worked example
Is a third machine worth it?
For example, Hauwa in Kano considers a third sewing machine, at about 60 extra bags a month.
One-time cost
Extra contribution a month
Extra running costs a month
Naira prices are approximate.

Expand at the bottleneck. For Hauwa that is sewing, so she prices a third machine. Capacity would rise to 792 bags a month, but she does not assume she will sell them all. From buyer conversations she expects about 60 extra bags at first.
The machine, table and socket cost about 500,000 naira. The extra bags bring 180,000 naira a month. A third machinist and power cost 85,000.
That leaves 95,000 naira extra profit a month. Payback is one-time cost divided by extra monthly profit: about 5.3 months.
Test the bad case
What if sales are weaker?
60 extra bags
95,000 naira a month profit
Payback about 5.3 months
30 extra bags
5,000 naira a month profit
Payback 100 months
On cautious sales, the machine pays for itself in about five to six months.

But if she sells only 30 extra bags, profit drops to 5,000 naira a month, and payback becomes 100 months. That is why she waits for confirmed orders and a deposit before buying. Never borrow against a full-capacity forecast.
Your 90 days
Days 1-30: confirm demand, get quotes
Write your plan in four phases. Confirm demand before buying. Then install, with a safe socket and a place that keeps the walkway clear.
Leave time to hire and train before you rely on the new capacity, and update your risk assessment. At day 90, review output, sales, running costs and incidents.
Key points
Remember
Check capacity, cash and quality before yes
Train in four steps; cross-train key tasks
Expand at the bottleneck
Payback = one-time cost / extra monthly profit

To remember. Check capacity, cash and quality before you say yes. Cross-train so no task depends on one person. Expand at the bottleneck, work out payback on cautious sales, and test it against a bad case.
